newsitem.title: GERMANY: Cloning wakes German memories of Nazi master race.
newsitem.headline: Cloning wakes German memories of Nazi master race.

text.p: Haunted by memories of Nazi attempts to breed a "superhuman" race, Germans are reacting to news that Scottish scientists have cloned sheep with a peculiar mixture of horror and humour.

Government ministers rushed to assure an alarmed public that humans would never be cloned, while scholars and editorial writers warned on Thursday that cloning a sheep was a scientific breakthrough of the same magnitude as the atomic bomb.

Newspapers such as Munich's Abendzeitung took a lighter approach, printing five identical pictures of a smiling Chancellor Helmut Kohl over a front page banner headline that read: "Genetic researchers say they could now clone Kohl."

Already deeply suspicious and fiercely opposed to genetic manipulation used even on simple agricultural products such as tomatoes and soyabeans, Germany has some of the world's most restrictive laws on genetic engineering.
Surrogate motherhood is even outlawed here.

Reflecting its shame over the Nazis' horrific experiments on humans, Germany keeps its multi-billion dollar pharmaceutical industry on a tight leash, applying strict bans on research that is widely practised in the United States and other countries.
"Germans are extremely sensitive to the issue," Peter Benninghoff-Luehl, an expert on genetic engineering at the Konrad Adenauer Institute think tank, told Reuters.
"Because of our history, there would be near-unanimous outrage here if anyone ever tried to clone a human."

Under Adolf Hitler, German scientists -- who were among the most respected in the world before the Nazi era -- took part in an ignominious attempt to create an Aryan blue-eyed and blond-haired "master race".

The Nazis also adopted the "science" of eugenics, which proclaimed that some were fit to live and breed while others, such as the mentally or physically handicapped, were considered genetically inferior and had to be destroyed or sterilised.

"The cloning of human beings would fit precisely into Adolf Hitler's world view," wrote the daily Die Welt. "And there is no doubt that he would have used this technology intensively if it were available at that time. Thank God it wasn't."

Die Welt worried that even if nations promised not to use the technology to clone humans, that was no guarantee that strong personalities with big egos and enough wealth could clone themselves surreptitiously.
"No one can build an atomic bomb in their garage, but genetic technology supported with the right know-how could create something that could move the world," the paper said.
Even the conservative business daily Handelsblatt leaped into the story on Thursday with three lengthy articles.
"The genetic coup of Edinburgh is more than anything else an ethics question," Handelsblatt said.

"With the cloning of an adult creature, humans can put an end to evolution. We have crossed a barrier we should have left standing. The birth of the sheep Dolly is an event not unlike the first nuclear explosion."
The liberal weekly newspaper Die Zeit noted that it may some day be possible for women to reproduce without any contribution from men, whose genes could become superfluous.
"How long will it take now until a new Einstein, Lollobrigida or even Hitler populates the brave new world?"
The ARD television network warned the experiment in Scotland was "politically dangerous".
"We are not talking about a toothache, but rather human dignity," ARD said in a commentary. "What would the Nazis have done if the possibility of human cloning were available then?"

Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung newspaper elected to inform its readers of an important detail. It said the sheep was named "Dolly" after the buxom American country-western singer Dolly Parton because a sheep's breast cell was used for the clone.
